patient.name: Desmond Clarke
patient.complaint: Agonising, hot, swollen right big toe since 3 am
background: BMI 32; drinks 4 pints of beer most weekends

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an acute red hot 1st MTP joint or knee, often with synovial fluid crystals given: needle and negative means gout, rhomboid and positive means pseudogout.

points: Desmond woke at **3 am** with agonising pain in his right big toe.
He cannot bear the **bedsheet** touching it.
Long hot weekend, lots of beer, little water.
No injury, no wound, no previous episodes.

steps.lead: A sudden, exquisitely painful single joint in a middle-aged man: think **crystal arthropathy** first, and gout is the urate type.
Desmond has three risk factors on one page: **male**, **CKD** and a **thiazide** (bendroflumethiazide), plus weekend **dehydration**.

points: Right **1st MTP joint**: red, shiny, swollen, exquisitely tender.
Redness confined to the joint; no tracking up the foot.
Other joints normal; no skin break.
No nodules on his ears or elbows.

steps.lead: Big toe, sudden, distal, one joint: the textbook **gout** monoarthropathy. Pseudogout would favour Desmond's knee or wrist.

steps.q: Desmond has an acute red hot 1st MTP joint and takes a thiazide. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: Sudden **1st MTP** monoarthritis plus thiazide, CKD and dehydration is **gout**. Pseudogout prefers large joints; cellulitis spreads beyond the joint.

Gout

steps.lead: Desmond has no **tophi** yet. Years of untreated attacks would leave chalky urate nodules on his **pinnae** and extensor surfaces.
An X-ray of Desmond's foot today would show only **soft tissue swelling**; punched-out erosions come with **recurrent** gout.
Desmond is 61 with obvious causes. In a **young boy** with gout, self-injury and developmental delay, think **Lesch-Nyhan**.

steps.text: A hot swollen joint with **fever** is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Crystals and infection can coexist, so the aspirate needs **Gram stain and culture** too.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (joint aspiration with polarised light microscopy) or a synovial fluid report where the crystal shape and birefringence decide gout versus pseudogout.

o: Joint aspiration with polarised light microscopy
steps.r: **Synovial fluid analysis** shows the crystals themselves. Urate supports the diagnosis but can be normal in an attack.

steps.r: NSAIDs are contraindicated in **CKD stage 3**, so **colchicine**. Allopurinol and febuxostat are long-term prophylaxis, not for the acute attack.

steps.text: Do not start allopurinol **during** the acute attack. But if a patient already takes it and flares, **continue** it and treat the flare.
Review the cause: Desmond's **thiazide** raises urate, so his antihypertensive is switched (losartan is a sensible alternative). Advise fluids and less beer.

steps.lead: Desmond **underexcretes** urate (CKD plus thiazide), so it rises until crystals precipitate in his cool, distal toe joint.

steps.title: From purines to a hot toe
nodes: Hyperuricaemia: urate crystals in synovial fluid
Neutrophil influx: hot, red, swollen joint
steps.caption: Allopurinol blocks step 3; colchicine damps the neutrophil step.

steps.lead: Desmond's **allopurinol** blocks **xanthine oxidase**, so less xanthine becomes uric acid and his serum urate falls.

steps.q: How does Desmond's colchicine reduce the inflammation?
steps.r: Colchicine inhibits **microtubule polymerisation**, reducing neutrophil migration and phagocytosis. NSAIDs inhibit COX; allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase.

steps.lead: With fewer neutrophils reaching and swallowing crystals, Desmond's acute **inflammatory response** is dampened.
Starting allopurinol mid-attack would **mobilise urate stores** and could prolong Desmond's flare; hence the 2-week wait and colchicine cover.

visual.caption: Dose titrated until urate is below the 360 µmol/L target; no further attacks.

steps.lead: Pseudogout is different chemistry: **calcium pyrophosphate** in cartilage, linked to ageing, hyperparathyroidism and haemochromatosis rather than urate.

steps.text: Urate crystals form more easily in **cool**, peripheral joints, which is one reason the **big toe** is the classic site.

mcq.q: Which joint is most commonly affected in gout?
mcq.r: Gout classically affects the **1st MTP joint** (podagra); pseudogout prefers the knee and wrist.

mcq.q: Which drug class is a classic precipitant of gout?
mcq.r: **Thiazides** (bendroflumethiazide, indapamide) reduce urate excretion. Pyrazinamide and ethambutol also raise urate.

mcq.q: Which X-ray finding is characteristic of pseudogout?
mcq.r: **Chondrocalcinosis** (calcified cartilage) is pseudogout. Punched-out erosions are recurrent gout.

mcq.q: Which condition is associated with pseudogout?
mcq.r: Pseudogout is linked to **haemochromatosis**, hyperparathyroidism and acromegaly.

mcq.q: What crystals are seen in gout under polarised light?
mcq.r: Monosodium urate crystals are **needle-shaped and negatively birefringent**.

mcq.q: What is the most useful test to confirm gout?
o: Joint aspiration and synovial fluid analysis
mcq.r: **Synovial fluid analysis** shows the urate crystals directly.

mcq.q: Which is the first-line urate-lowering drug after a gout attack?
mcq.r: **Allopurinol** first-line; **febuxostat** second-line if not tolerated. Colchicine and naproxen treat the attack.

mcq.q: How long is NSAID or colchicine cover given when starting allopurinol?
mcq.r: **3 months** of cover reduces the flare risk while urate stores are mobilised.

mcq.q: What is the mechanism of allopurinol?
mcq.r: Allopurinol (and febuxostat) inhibit **xanthine oxidase**, reducing uric acid production.

glossary.Crystal arthropathy: Joint disease caused by crystals depositing in and around the joint, mainly gout and pseudogout.
glossary.Gout: Inflammatory arthritis caused by monosodium urate crystals forming when blood urate is high.
glossary.Pseudogout: Acute arthritis caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals, usually in the knee or wrist of older people.
glossary.Hyperuricaemia: A raised level of uric acid (urate) in the blood.
glossary.Monosodium urate: The salt of uric acid that forms the needle-shaped crystals of gout.
glossary.Calcium pyrophosphate: The calcium salt that forms the rhomboid crystals of pseudogout.
glossary.CPPD: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, the umbrella term that includes pseudogout.
glossary.1st MTP: First metatarsophalangeal joint, at the base of the big toe; the classic site of gout.
glossary.Tophi: Chalky lumps of urate crystals under the skin, on the ears or over joints, in long-standing gout.
glossary.Chronic tophaceous gout: Long-standing gout with tophi and joint damage from years of high urate.
glossary.Pinnae: The visible outer parts of the ears.
glossary.Birefringence: How a crystal bends polarised light; positive or negative birefringence helps identify the crystal type.
glossary.Polarised light microscopy: Microscopy with polarised light, used on joint fluid to identify crystals by shape and birefringence.
glossary.Synovial fluid: The lubricating fluid inside a joint, sampled by aspiration.
glossary.Joint aspiration: Drawing fluid out of a joint with a needle for analysis.
glossary.Chondrocalcinosis: Calcium deposits visible in joint cartilage on X-ray, typical of pseudogout.
glossary.Punched-out erosions: Sharply defined bone erosions near joints on X-ray, seen in recurrent gout.
glossary.Subchondral sclerosis: Increased density of the bone just beneath the cartilage.
glossary.Lesch-Nyhan syndrome: Rare X-linked recessive disorder of purine metabolism causing high urate, gout, self-injury and developmental delay.
glossary.Haemochromatosis: Inherited iron overload causing liver disease, diabetes, bronze skin and pseudogout.
glossary.Hyperparathyroidism: Overactive parathyroid glands causing high calcium; associated with pseudogout.
glossary.Acromegaly: Excess growth hormone in adults, causing enlarged hands, feet and jaw.
glossary.Bendroflumethiazide: A thiazide diuretic used for hypertension that reduces urate excretion and can trigger gout.
glossary.Pyrazinamide: An anti-tuberculosis drug that raises serum urate.
glossary.Colchicine: Anti-inflammatory drug for acute gout that blocks microtubules; causes diarrhoea and vomiting.
glossary.Allopurinol: First-line urate-lowering drug that inhibits xanthine oxidase.
glossary.Febuxostat: Second-line xanthine oxidase inhibitor used if allopurinol is not tolerated.
glossary.Xanthine oxidase: Enzyme that converts hypoxanthine and xanthine into uric acid.
glossary.NLRP3 inflammasome: An immune protein complex that senses urate crystals and releases IL-1β.
glossary.IL-1β: Interleukin-1 beta, a cytokine that drives the inflammation of a gout attack.
glossary.Microtubule: Protein tubes inside cells needed for neutrophil movement; blocked by colchicine.
glossary.G6PD deficiency: Inherited enzyme deficiency in which some drugs trigger haemolysis of red cells.
glossary.Stevens-Johnson syndrome: A severe, life-threatening blistering reaction of skin and mucous membranes, usually drug-induced.
glossary.Urate-lowering therapy: Long-term drugs (allopurinol, febuxostat) that lower serum urate to prevent gout attacks.
glossary.NSAIDs: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, such as naproxen and diclofenac, which inhibit cyclo-oxygenase.
glossary.PPI: Proton pump inhibitor, such as omeprazole, given to protect the stomach with NSAIDs.
glossary.CKD: Chronic kidney disease, graded 1 to 5 by eGFR.
glossary.eGFR: Estimated glomerular filtration rate, a measure of kidney function.

technique.stem: A 64 year old man has a 1 day history of a painful, swollen right big toe. The pain woke him at night. He takes bendroflumethiazide for hypertension. His temperature is 37.3°C. The right first metatarsophalangeal joint is red, swollen and exquisitely tender. Synovial fluid microscopy shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. Gram stain shows no organisms.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about a single hot joint: decide crystal versus infection, then which crystal.
Thiazide raises urate; 1st MTP is the classic gout joint; needle and negative is urate; no organisms argues against infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Acute 1st MTP monoarthritis with urate crystals: **gout**.

elim: Pseudogout crystals are rhomboid and positively birefringent, and favour the knee.
Reactive arthritis follows infection and has no crystals.
Rheumatoid is a symmetrical small joint polyarthritis.
Septic arthritis has organisms or pus; Gram stain is clear and there is no fever.

steps.x: **A. Gout.** Rule: needle and negative = urate = gout.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pseudogout = calcium pyrophosphate = **rhomboid, positively birefringent**.

elim: Cocci would mean septic arthritis; Gram stain is clear.
Needle and negative is gout.
Mixes gout's shape with pseudogout's birefringence.
Right shape, wrong sign: CPP crystals are positive.

steps.x: **E. Rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals.** Rule: P for pyrophosphate, P for positive.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Allopurinol is prophylaxis, started about 2 weeks after the attack.
Febuxostat is second-line prophylaxis, not acute treatment.

Naproxen is an NSAID: contraindicated in CKD 3.

technique.stem: A 58 year old man has had three attacks of gout in the past year. He has tophi on both ear helices. Two weeks after his latest attack has settled he is started on a low dose of a drug that is titrated up until his serum urate falls below 360 µmol/L.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

practice.stem: A 59 year old man has a 12 hour history of severe pain in his right big toe. He cannot bear his sock touching it. He drinks 30 units of alcohol a week. His temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 150/92 mmHg. The first metatarsophalangeal joint is red, shiny and swollen.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Acute 1st MTP monoarthritis with needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals is gout. Septic arthritis would show organisms; pseudogout crystals are rhomboid and positive.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a single hot joint with a synovial fluid report.

clues: cannot bear his sock touching it
steps.x: Big toe, alcohol, exquisite tenderness; the fluid shows urate crystals and no organisms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Needle and negative: **gout**.

elim: Cellulitis spreads beyond the joint and has no crystals.
Pseudogout crystals are rhomboid and positively birefringent.
Reactive arthritis follows GI or GU infection; no crystals.
No organisms on Gram stain and only a low-grade temperature.

steps.x: **B. Gout.** Rule: the crystal report decides it.

practice.stem: A 78 year old woman has a 3 day history of a painful, swollen left knee. She can still walk with a stick. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 134/78 mmHg. practice.e: Rhomboid positively birefringent crystals in an older woman's knee with chondrocalcinosis is pseudogout. Gout crystals are needle-shaped and negative.

steps.x: **C. Pseudogout.** Rule: rhomboid, positive, chondrocalcinosis.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has a 1 day history of a hot, swollen right ankle. He had a similar episode in his big toe 3 years ago. practice.q: Which drug most likely precipitated this attack?
practice.e: Thiazide diuretics such as bendroflumethiazide reduce urate excretion and precipitate gout. Losartan, if anything, lowers urate.

steps.x: It asks for the cause: which drug raises urate?

clues: similar episode in his big toe

Lisinopril, an ACE inhibitor, is not a classic cause.

steps.x: **A. Bendroflumethiazide.** Rule: new gout + new antihypertensive = thiazide.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has had recurrent attacks of joint pain in his feet and hands for 15 years and has never taken regular medication for them. He has chronic kidney disease. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 142/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
practice.e: Long-standing untreated hyperuricaemia gives chronic tophaceous gout, with urate tophi on the pinnae and extensor surfaces. Swan-neck and ulnar deviation are rheumatoid.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Tophi** on the pinnae and extensor surfaces.

Nail pitting suggests psoriatic arthritis.
Swan-neck deformity is rheumatoid arthritis.
Ulnar deviation is rheumatoid arthritis.

steps.x: **D. Tophi on the ear helices.** Rule: long untreated gout = tophi.

practice.stem: A 48 year old man has a 2 day history of a hot, swollen right knee. He has type 2 diabetes diagnosed last year and tanned skin despite not travelling. The liver edge is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. Knee aspirate shows positively birefringent rhomboid crystals.
practice.q: Which underlying condition is most likely?
practice.e: Pseudogout in a younger man with diabetes, bronze skin, hepatomegaly and iron overload points to haemochromatosis, a recognised cause of CPPD.

steps.x: A cause question: young pseudogout needs a metabolic reason.
Pseudogout + diabetes + bronze skin + hepatomegaly, and transferrin saturation 78%.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Iron overload: **haemochromatosis**.

elim: Alcohol does not cause bronze diabetes or CPPD.
Fatty liver does not give transferrin saturation of 78% or bronze skin.
PBC is cholestatic, in middle-aged women, with itch.
Sarcoid gives hypercalcaemia and lung disease, not iron overload.

steps.x: **B. Haemochromatosis.** Rule: pseudogout + diabetes + big liver = check iron.

practice.stem: A 67 year old man has had gout for 12 years with frequent attacks in his left foot. He stopped allopurinol years ago. His temperature is 36.9°C and pulse rate 72 bpm. An X-ray of the left foot is performed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on X-ray?

steps.x: Imaging finding of long-standing recurrent gout.
Recurrent, poorly controlled gout: bone damage is expected.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Punched-out erosions** with sclerosis.

elim: Chondrocalcinosis is pseudogout.
Joint space loss and osteophytes are osteoarthritis; gout preserves joint space.
Pencil-in-cup is psoriatic arthritis.
Periarticular osteopenia is early rheumatoid arthritis.

steps.x: **E. Punched-out erosions.** Rule: gout punches, pseudogout calcifies.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man has a 1 day history of a hot, swollen right knee. He has had gout in his big toe before. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Joint aspiration and synovial fluid analysis
practice.e: Joint aspiration with Gram stain, culture and polarised microscopy confirms crystals and excludes septic arthritis. Serum urate cannot exclude infection and may be normal in an attack.

steps.x: 'Diagnostic' means the test that confirms it.

clues: gout in his big toe before
steps.x: Likely gout, but a fever means sepsis must be excluded too.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Aspirate the joint**: crystals and Gram stain in one test.

elim: MRI is not needed to diagnose an acute crystal arthritis.
Rheumatoid factor is for rheumatoid arthritis.
Urate supports gout but does not exclude infection.
X-ray is often normal in an acute attack.

steps.x: **A. Joint aspiration.** Rule: hot joint = aspirate.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man sees his GP with a 2 day history of a painful, red, swollen left big toe. He takes indapamide. He is otherwise well. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 144/90 mmHg. The GP suspects gout and joint aspiration is not available in the practice.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: NICE recommends serum urate alongside the clinical picture to confirm gout in primary care. Repeat it at least 2 weeks after the flare if it is normal.

steps.x: Initial test, in general practice, without aspiration.
Classic gout, thiazide-like diuretic, systemically well.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Serum urate** with the clinical features.

elim: Anti-CCP is for rheumatoid arthritis.
He is afebrile and well; no sepsis suspected.
Rheumatoid factor is for rheumatoid arthritis.
X-ray is usually normal in a first attack.

steps.x: **D. Serum urate.** Rule: NICE first-line is urate plus the clinical picture.

practice.stem: A 57 year old man has had his first attack of gout, treated with naproxen. He has chronic kidney disease stage 3. The attack settled completely 3 days ago. His GP wants to start urate-lowering therapy.
practice.q: When is the most appropriate time to start allopurinol?
o: In about 2 weeks, at a low dose
practice.e: Allopurinol is offered after the first attack, started about 2 weeks after it at a low dose and titrated up. Starting too early can mobilise urate and trigger a flare.

steps.x: Timing and dose of urate-lowering therapy.
CKD 3 is an indication; the attack has only just settled.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Wait about **2 weeks**, then start **low** and titrate.

elim: Allopurinol is offered after the first attack.
Too early and too high a dose risks a flare.
CKD 3 is a NICE indication for urate-lowering therapy.
Six months is an unnecessary delay.

steps.x: **C. In about 2 weeks, at a low dose.** Rule: wait, start low, titrate, cover.

practice.stem: A 60 year old woman with recurrent gout is starting allopurinol 2 weeks after her latest attack. She has no kidney disease. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate additional prescription?
practice.e: When starting allopurinol, NSAID or colchicine cover is given for 3 months to reduce flares as urate stores mobilise. Febuxostat replaces allopurinol; it is not added.

steps.x: What goes alongside allopurinol when it is started?
Initiation phase: high flare risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anti-inflammatory cover: **colchicine (or NSAID) for 3 months**.

elim: A thiazide raises urate and worsens gout.
Febuxostat is an alternative to allopurinol, never combined.
A year of steroids is not cover; it causes harm.
Rasburicase is for tumour lysis syndrome.

steps.x: **B. Colchicine for 3 months.** Rule: allopurinol always starts with cover.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man has an acute attack of gout in his right ankle. He had a bleeding duodenal ulcer last year and takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. Colchicine last year caused severe diarrhoea and he refuses it. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 82 bpm irregular and BP 138/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: NSAIDs are contraindicated (peptic bleed, elderly on warfarin) and colchicine was not tolerated, so a corticosteroid is the next choice for the acute attack.

steps.x: Acute treatment: look for contraindications to the first-line drugs.
NSAIDs out (bleed, warfarin); colchicine out (intolerance).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Neither first-line option: **corticosteroid**.

elim: Allopurinol is not for the acute attack.
He could not tolerate colchicine and refuses it.
Diclofenac is an NSAID: bleed risk with warfarin and ulcer history.
Naproxen is an NSAID: same contraindications.

steps.x: **E. Oral prednisolone.** Rule: no NSAID and no colchicine = steroid.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man with an acute attack of gout is treated with colchicine. Two days later his joint is much better but he has developed diarrhoea. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the mechanism of action of the drug that reduced his joint inflammation?
practice.e: Colchicine inhibits microtubule polymerisation, reducing neutrophil migration and phagocytosis of urate crystals. Xanthine oxidase inhibition is allopurinol.

steps.x: Mechanism of colchicine.
Colchicine works fast on inflammation; diarrhoea is its classic side effect.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Colchicine blocks **microtubules**, so neutrophils cannot migrate and phagocytose.

elim: IL-6 receptor blockade is tocilizumab.
COX inhibition is NSAIDs.
Phospholipase A2 inhibition is a corticosteroid action.
Xanthine oxidase inhibition is allopurinol and febuxostat.

steps.x: **C. Inhibits microtubule polymerisation.** Rule: colchicine = microtubules = neutrophils.
